content: A blood bank is a facility where blood or its components, collected through blood donation, are stored and preserved for future use in transfusions. In 1915, Richard Lewison at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York introduced sodium citrate as an anticoagulant, which revolutionized blood transfusion by enabling indirect transfusion rather than direct vein-to-vein transfer. That same year, Richard Weil demonstrated that anticoagulated blood could be stored under refrigeration. In 1917, Francis Peyton Rous and J.R. Turner developed a citrate-glucose solution, allowing blood to be stored in containers for several days. This advancement led to the establishment of the first blood depot in Britain during World War I. Oswald Hope Robertson, a U.S. Army officer and medical researcher, is credited with creating the first blood bank by organizing these depots. By the mid-1930s, the Soviet Union had developed an extensive system of blood centers, with at least 60 major facilities and over 500 smaller ones, storing and distributing canned blood across the country. This model inspired Bernard Fantus, the director of therapeutics at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, to establish the first hospital blood bank in the United States in 1937. Fantus also coined the term blood bank. Within a few years, similar hospital and community blood banks were established across the U.S. In Europe, Willem Johan Kolff organized the first blood bank in 1940. A significant advancement occurred between 1939 and 1940 when Karl Landsteiner, Alex Wiener, Philip Levine, and R.E. Stetson discovered the Rh blood group system, which was responsible for most transfusion reactions at the time. In 1943, J.F. Loutit and Patrick L. Mollison introduced the acid-citrate-dextrose (ACD) solution, which reduced the volume of anticoagulant needed, enabling larger transfusions and longer storage durations. In 1950, Carl Walter and W.P. Murphy, Jr., introduced plastic bags for blood collection, replacing fragile glass bottles. This innovation allowed for safer and more efficient preparation of multiple blood components from a single unit of whole blood. In 1979, the anticoagulant preservative CPDA-1 was introduced, further extending the shelf life of stored blood and improving resource sharing among blood banks. Modern solutions containing adenine now allow red blood cells to be stored for up to 42 days. Red blood cells can also be frozen by combining them with a glycerol solution to prevent ice crystal formation. Frozen red blood cells have a shelf life of up to 10 years, but the process is costly and labor-intensive, so only a few blood banks maintain frozen stocks. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) can be stored for up to one year if kept frozen. Platelets, however, are typically stored at room temperature and have a shelf life of only five days due to the high risk of bacterial contamination. Experimental bacteriological screening protocols may extend this to seven days. The AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) provides a Circular of Information, which serves as a detailed guide on the use and handling of blood products.
